archived.reason: The last release, 1.1.13, came out in October 2023 and the last commit in May 2024. A Yatai 2.0 for BentoML 1.2, proposed in February 2024 with a beta planned for autumn 2024, never shipped, and the repository was archived and made read-only on 11 June 2026.

summary: A Kubernetes operator and web console for deploying BentoML services, with custom resources for building Bento images and running them as autoscaled deployments. Archived in June 2026; it never supported BentoML 1.2’s service API.
intro: Yatai (屋台, a Japanese food cart) took Bentos, the packaged services that BentoML builds, and ran them on any Kubernetes cluster. It came in three parts. Yatai itself was a web UI and API with a central registry for Bentos and models, user accounts and API tokens; its quick install also set up PostgreSQL for metadata and MinIO for storage. yatai-image-builder added the `Bento` and `BentoRequest` custom resources and built a container image from a Bento inside the cluster. yatai-deployment added the `BentoDeployment` resource, which turned a Bento into Kubernetes deployments, services and ingress.

Developers pushed a Bento with `bentoml push`, and DevOps teams deployed it either from the UI or by applying a `BentoDeployment` manifest, which fit GitOps tools and CI pipelines. In BentoML 1.0 and 1.1 a service was split into an API server and Runners that did the model inference, and Yatai gave each Runner its own pods, resources and autoscaling range, so a GPU model could scale separately from CPU preprocessing. Version 1.0 also wired in Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, Loki for logs, and tracing through Zipkin, Jaeger or OpenTelemetry.

BentoML 1.2 (February 2024) introduced service classes in place of Runners, and Yatai never caught up: its README says “Yatai for BentoML 1.2 is currently under construction”. The repository was archived on 11 June 2026. The separate yatai-deployment repository still receives CI and Go version updates, but the project as a whole is no longer developed.
strengths: Kubernetes-native: a `BentoDeployment` is a custom resource you apply with `kubectl`, review in Git and roll out with existing CI/CD
Separate autoscaling and hardware for each Runner, so preprocessing stays on cheap CPU nodes while the model scales on GPU nodes
Builds images inside the cluster from a pushed Bento, so data scientists never write a Dockerfile
One place to see Bentos, models, deployments, metrics and logs, with a web UI for teams who don’t use `kubectl`
limits: Archived since June 2026, with no release since October 2023 and no support for BentoML 1.2 and later
Heavy to install: its own users’ top complaint was setup, with stateful components such as a database and several namespaces, and a user system that didn’t fit Kubernetes RBAC
Elastic License 2.0, not an open-source license; the planned move to Apache 2.0 came with the 2.0 rewrite that never shipped
In-cluster image building was hard to optimize and debug, and teams asked to deploy their own prebuilt images instead

story: BentoML packaged a model and its code into a Bento, but teams then had to run it at scale themselves. They asked for multi-model deployments, scalable inference graphs and a central model store for collaboration, noting that storing models in S3 “doesn’t scale forever”. BentoML started Yatai in mid-2021 as an open-source system for running those deployments on Kubernetes, and released Yatai 1.0 in November 2022, with separate autoscaling groups per Runner, Prometheus and Grafana dashboards, log shipping with Loki and GitOps deployments through a custom resource. Mission Lane and CJ Express wrote about running it, and Kubeflow documented an integration.

In February 2024, the same month BentoML 1.2 changed its programming model, the team published a Yatai 2.0 proposal. It listed what users had learned: setup was too intrusive, the in-cluster image builder was hard to optimize, stateful components were either expensive or unreliable, and the Elastic License limited partners. The plan was a single `BentoDeployment` controller installed with Helm, no database, support for custom registries and an S3-based model store, a move to Apache 2.0, and a beta in September or October 2024.

The beta never appeared. The proposal issue stayed open, and a user asked in July 2025 whether it was still in development. After Modular bought BentoML in February 2026, the Yatai repository was archived on 11 June 2026.

choices.choice: Custom resources instead of a deployment script
choices.why: DevOps teams already managed everything through Kubernetes manifests and GitOps. A `BentoDeployment` resource let a model service go through the same review, CI and rollback process as any other workload.

In a typical service, preprocessing and each model have different bottlenecks and hardware needs. Splitting a Bento into separately scaled pods let GPU nodes run only the models and cheaper CPU nodes run the rest.

Data scientists push a Bento, not a container, so the platform built the image for them. In practice this became the part users found hardest to debug, and the 2.0 plan was to accept prebuilt images instead.

timeline.text: Yatai 2.0 proposal (February); last commit to the main repository (May)
